The design guide

The reasoning, tradeoffs, page structure, and feature priorities behind the visual options.

What the current site gives us

The existing site has useful foundations: a short introduction, focused Research / Experience / CV navigation, substantial publication content, original research figures, direct resource links, and an interactive map of your work.

Current detailProposed improvementBenefit
Homepage order is introduction → scrolling news → research map → highlightsSplit introduction → illustrated research rows → scrolling news → more linksRestores the Research Index structure with the complete content
A permanent profile sidebar and several competing visual treatmentsUse a text-only split introduction; unify type, spacing, and accentClearer hierarchy and more reading space
News sits inside a small scrolling boxShow the latest three entries; scroll within the panel for the other 18Compact news with the complete history and keyboard access
Full paper titles, large figures, pills, borders, and shadows compete for attentionFull project title, original figure, concise summary, and quiet resource linksFaster scanning without losing depth
Research topic navigation disappears on smaller screensKeep a compact topic selector or wrapping controlsMobile visitors can still navigate the catalogue
Publication images have a fixed desktop width and use croppingResponsive figures with their full content visibleBetter mobile layout and legible scientific diagrams
Venue/status details are repeated across pages and the mapUse one publication record for all viewsFewer inconsistent updates

The selected Research Index uses a text-only introduction with name, affiliation, and contact links. Project figures remain part of each research entry.

Three design directions

Editorial

A centered reading column, a distinctive name heading, a short introduction, and selected research arranged as spacious rows. Serif headings give it a scholarly feel; the navigation and body remain simple.

  • Layout: top navigation, compact introduction, three illustrated projects, all existing updates, short contact footer.
  • Visual character: warm neutral background, forest accent, generous spacing, thin separators.
  • Figures: a full, uncropped image for every project, including on mobile.
  • Best fit: a personal academic website that feels considered and approachable.
  • Tradeoff: visitors looking for a specific older paper make one extra click to Research.

Alternative direction. Research Index is the selected homepage direction.

Research Index

The selected direction restores the original Research Index structure: top navigation, a split introduction, aligned research rows, and a compact news panel showing three entries. All 21 updates remain available by scrolling. The full biography, original project figures, and all resource links enrich that layout. Georgia headings, system sans body text, and the Paper and Ink palette provide the visual treatment.

  • Layout: top navigation; name and contact links beside the biography; Focus / Project / Resources rows; three visible news entries with earlier updates scrollable; research map, Experience, and CV links.
  • Visual character: warm paper background, forest links, Georgia headings, and aligned research entries.
  • Figures: an image for every project, preserving the original figures and their aspect ratios.
  • Best fit: frequent visitors, collaborators, and readers searching for papers or code.
  • Tradeoff: keeping every update makes the homepage longer; clear headings and dates make the list easier to scan.

Selected for the homepage and Research page. Keep the original Research Index structure and text-only identity, with complete research entries.

Quiet Sidebar

A refined version of the existing structure: a narrow identity rail on desktop and a generous research column. The profile becomes an inline introduction on mobile.

  • Layout: small artwork or portrait, name, affiliation, and contact links in a 200–220 px rail; selected work and updates in the main column.
  • Visual character: neutral palette, simple sans-serif type, minimal decoration.
  • Figures: consistent, uncropped figures for every project, with readable text alongside or above them.
  • Best fit: retaining the recognizable academic homepage format.
  • Tradeoff: two columns leave less space at tablet widths; avoid a separately scrolling sidebar.

Choose this if continuity with the current site matters most.

Color palettes

Each palette uses one background, one surface color, strong body text, readable secondary text, and one accent. The accent is for links, active controls, and keyboard focus. Research figures can retain their own colors.

TokenPaper and InkCool SlateWarm ClayMonochrome
Background#FAF9F6#F8FAFC#FBF8F4#FFFFFF
Raised or inset surface#FFFFFF#FFFFFF#FFFFFF#F5F5F4
Primary text#202124#172033#28231F#202020
Secondary text#62645F#586477#6B6058#626262
Accent#315C49#2459A6#984A32#3C3C3C
Decorative divider#DEDFD9#DAE1EA#E4DBD2#DEDEDA
ImpressionWarm, understated, scholarlyCrisp, technical, familiarPersonal, warm, distinctiveQuiet, flexible, typographic

Paper and Ink is the recommended balance. Cool Slate is the closest continuation of the current blue links. Warm Clay gives the site more personality while staying restrained. Monochrome leaves almost all visual expression to type and research imagery.

Calculated contrast against each palette’s background:

PalettePrimary textSecondary textAccent text
Paper and Ink15.29:15.69:17.23:1
Cool Slate15.55:15.73:16.57:1
Warm Clay14.69:15.77:15.90:1
Monochrome16.29:16.10:111.03:1

All listed text colors also exceed 4.5:1 on their paired surface color. These are calculations for the exact, fully opaque tokens, not a full accessibility audit. Normal text needs at least 4.5:1 contrast under WCAG contrast guidance. The pale dividers are decorative; use the accent or a stronger neutral for essential control boundaries and focus indicators. Underline inline links so color is not their only identifier.

Optional dark appearance

Use a dark charcoal background rather than pure black. Start from background #171A19, surface #202422, text #F2F1EB, secondary text #B7BEB7, and decorative divider #3B423E. Match the palette with forest #A3C9B1, blue #A8C9FF, clay #EDBAA5, or neutral #DADADA accents.

Follow the system preference and optionally offer System / Light / Dark. Preserve white backgrounds inside scientific figures when needed; do not invert the images. This can follow the first redesign rather than delaying the content and layout improvements.

Typography
OptionHeadingsBody and navigationCharacter and tradeoff
Editorial pairingSource Serif 4InterScholarly and personal; two font families to load
Clear sansInterInterCohesive and quiet; less distinctive but easy to maintain
TechnicalIBM Plex SansIBM Plex Sans; Plex Mono only for dates or codeA little more engineering character; too much mono would make reading harder
Native and classicGeorgiaSystem sans-serifNo webfont downloads; appearance varies by device

Selected: Georgia for your name and major section headings; system sans-serif for body copy, long paper titles, navigation, and resource links. Use regular and medium/semibold weights; avoid thin text. Keep long paper titles in sans-serif even when the main headings are serif.

Suggested starting scale:

ElementDesktopMobileTreatment
Name / page title40–44 px32–36 pxCompact line height, natural wrapping
Section heading24–28 px22–24 pxClear separation from the section above
Project title19–21 px18–20 pxMedium weight
Body17–18 px16–17 pxLine height around 1.6
Metadata and links14–15 px14–15 pxFull-opacity readable color

Keep prose around 60–70 characters per line and left-align it. Use relative units in implementation so browser zoom and text settings continue to work. Prefer one or two font families, load only needed styles, and use a fallback while webfonts load.

Font references: Inter, Source Serif, and IBM Plex.

Website structure

Keep the main navigation small: Research · Experience · CV. The name links home. Place name, affiliation, Email, Scholar, GitHub, LinkedIn, and X in the left half of the introduction, with the biography on the right. Stack these blocks on mobile. Keep the CV link visible.

Home

  1. Split introduction. Name, affiliation, and contact links on the left; the full biography with advisor, YCL role, and undergraduate background on the right.
  2. Selected research. Focus / Project / Resources columns for TimeWarp, FrugalPrompt, and R-MMA. Each entry retains its original figure, full title, summary, and links.
  3. News and Updates. Show the latest three entries, newest first. Scroll within the keyboard-accessible panel to read the remaining 18; every entry and link is retained.
  4. More about the work. Research Map, Experience, and CV links follow the updates.
  5. Contact. A short footer keeps email easy to reach.

On mobile, stack the name and contact links, biography, illustrated research entries, scrolling news panel, and additional links in that order. Keep an image for every project at every viewport size. Let scientific figures retain their natural aspect ratio and open at full size.

Research

Make this the complete catalogue at the existing /publications/ address. Default to newest first, with a clear year and venue/status on each entry. If topic grouping remains preferable, keep it as an explicit view choice rather than repeating papers in several sections.

Every paper entry should retain its image, full title, authors with your name highlighted, venue/year or preprint status, one sentence explaining the contribution, and existing resource links. Preserve all 17 current publication figures when applying this design to Research. Abstract and BibTeX can expand beneath the entry. Stable anchors such as #timewarp make individual papers easy to share.

Start with a topic selector; add title/author search if browsing the full list still feels slow. Keep all papers readable without JavaScript. Filters should reveal matches, report the result count, and offer a clear reset and empty state.

Keep a Research Map section after the news panel. Preserve its connections and functionality, support keyboard use, and allow the page to scroll normally over it. The design explorer links to the current map; the actual graph remains part of the website implementation.

Experience

Use a simple chronological list for education, research/academic roles, and industry roles. Each entry needs role, organization, dates, and at most one or two lines of relevant context. Avoid progress bars, skill percentages, and decorative timeline graphics.

Keep /teaching/ working. If the URL becomes /experience/, add a redirect from the old route. Keep the existing PDF CV link working independently.

Additional pages

Add Writing only when there is original material ready to publish. A separate Projects page would overlap heavily with Research. Keep all existing updates in the homepage news panel, with three initially visible. A future archive may be an additional view, but should not replace or truncate this list.

Components and visual details
ComponentProposed rule
Page widthAbout 960–1040 px overall; narrower prose within it
SpacingUse a small shared scale: 8, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64 px
Section gapsRoughly 56–72 px on desktop; 36–48 px on mobile
Project rowsSeparate with whitespace or one subtle rule; use 24–32 px vertical padding
ThumbnailsOne image for every project; use the available content width for homepage figures and preserve the full image
Image treatmentNatural aspect ratio, no ornamental shadow; small 4–6 px radius if helpful
Identity imageText-only identity: name, affiliation, and contact links in the split introduction
LinksDescriptive text; underlined in prose; keep Paper / Code / Dataset consistent
ButtonsReserve for actions such as Copy citation or expanding content; resource navigation can be plain links
IconsUse sparingly alongside labels; avoid a row of unexplained symbols
MotionBrief color/focus transitions; respect reduced motion; no moving background or automatic graph motion

Example selected-work entry:

TimeWarp
Evaluating web agents across temporal versions of websites.
Paper · Code · Dataset · Project

The complete title and venue belong in the full research entry. Keep resource order consistent across projects and omit unavailable links entirely. Do not make the whole row clickable when it contains several separate actions.

Useful functionality

Effort is relative within the existing Jekyll site: small means a focused content or component change; medium means coordinated data, UI, and responsive work. These are scope estimates, not delivery dates.

PriorityFeatureWhy it helpsEffort and dependency
First passResponsive paper rows and mobile topic navigationMakes the existing research usable on phonesMedium; shared publication component
First passThree visible updates, with the full history scrollablePreserves all dates and links in a compact, keyboard-accessible panelSmall; structured news entries and responsive panel sizing
First passConsistent Email, Scholar, GitHub, and CV accessMakes the key visitor actions obviousSmall
First passStable paper anchors and direct resource linksLets readers share and access work quicklySmall
First passAccurate page titles, descriptions, and social previewGives shared links a coherent identitySmall; choose an appropriate preview image
NextTopic/year filtering, then search if usefulHelps readers navigate the growing catalogueMedium; consistent publication data
NextExpand abstract and copy BibTeXHelps researchers evaluate and cite papersMedium; verified citation records, visible confirmation, selectable-text fallback
Optional laterSystem-aware dark appearanceOffers a comfortable alternativeMedium; check every component and figure
RetainResearch connections mapKeeps a distinctive way to browse related workMedium; accessible alternative and explicit connection meaning
OptionalWriting feed or RSSUseful if you publish research notes regularlyMedium; only after real content exists

Leave out a chatbot, visitor counter, animated introduction, embedded social feed, and elaborate page transitions. They add interface and upkeep without materially improving the main reading and research tasks.

Content and implementation considerations

Keep Jekyll for this redesign. The proposed layouts and features do not require a framework migration.

  • Move shared presentation out of the long inline page styles into a small set of reusable styles and components. Define colors, type, spacing, and widths centrally.
  • Use one source of publication data to generate selected work, the catalogue, and map details. Add structured news separately, linking entries to publications where relevant.
  • Reconcile publication statuses before copying them into the new design. For example, the homepage announces TimeWarp at NeurIPS 2026 and FrugalPrompt at LUHME at EMNLP 2026, while other views still use preprint labels. Verify the intended status once, then render it consistently.
  • Review unused starter pages and collection entries before launch. The old HTML CV contains “GitHub University,” although the visible CV navigation correctly points to your PDF. Hiding a navigation item does not remove its published route.
  • Replace the placeholder site description, remove the stray “Transparent Button” document markup, use meaningful page headings, and maintain the footer year.
  • Keep existing URLs, redirects, PDF paths, and publication links stable. Check them after the layout changes.

Relevant existing files: _pages/about.md, _pages/publications.html, _pages/teaching.html, _data/navigation.yml, _sass/_variables.scss, and _config.yml.

Quality bar for a later implementation

The page should reflow at 320 CSS pixels, remain usable at 200% zoom, and keep reading and navigation available by keyboard. Use meaningful image descriptions, visible focus, a skip link, sensible heading order, and comfortable tap targets. Scientific figures must remain understandable when thumbnails are small. W3C reflow guidance explains the narrow-screen behavior.

Keep primary content in the initial HTML. Load the retained map without delaying the main content, size images to prevent layout shifts, and optimize figures without making their text illegible. Verify desktop, tablet, phone, keyboard use, reduced motion, and both appearances if dark mode is included.

Suggested sequence
  1. Use the selected direction. Research Index, Paper and Ink, Georgia + system sans, light appearance, and a text-only introduction.
  2. Refresh the core experience. Restore the original Research Index sequence with the complete biography, research rows, and updates; then apply the same system to Research and Experience, preserving every project image. Address mobile reading and content inconsistencies together.
  3. Add focused tools. Introduce publication filters and citations when the shared catalogue is ready. Keep the map; consider dark appearance and writing afterward.
